contract: CBWeb3 Authentication and Session (shared, Scenario A + Scenario B)

vectors.title: Direct login returns tokens and sets the session cookie
vectors.description: A governance/supervisor/NOC participant authenticates with clientId + clientSecret. The gateway answers 200 with an AuthResponse and installs the access_token and refresh_token HttpOnly cookies via Set-Cookie. From this point the session is usable with no Authorization header.

preconditions.gateway: any CBWeb3 gateway (Scenario A or Scenario B)

vectors.notes: The cookie is the credential for the whole /api/v1 surface. tokenType is always the literal 'Bearer' in the delivered gateway, but the /api/v1 routes are guarded by CookieAuth, not by an Authorization header. refreshToken is optional and may be absent.

vectors.title: PKI login step 1 returns a nonce and no tokens
vectors.description: The same endpoint behaves differently for a commercial bank or treasury participant: it returns only {"nonce": "<hex>"}. No tokens are issued and no cookie is set. The client must sign the nonce and call POST /api/v1/auth/wallet/bind.
vectors.notes: Load-bearing upstream defect, mirrored not fixed: the platform types this 200 as AuthResponse, whose required properties are accessToken/expiresIn/tokenType and which has no nonce property. A strict OpenAPI response validator therefore FAILS a perfectly correct PKI login. The contract models the nonce branch as a documented oneOf carrying x-cbweb3-source: implementation-observed. The server chooses the flow from the participant's role; the client cannot request one.

vectors.title: PKI login step 2 — wallet bind issues the session
vectors.description: The client signs the nonce from auth-hp-02 with the P-256 private key matching its participant certificate, DER-encodes the signature and hex-encodes it, then posts it with the certificate PEM. This is how a commercial bank actually obtains a session.
vectors.notes: Public endpoint (security: []) because the signature over the nonce IS the credential. A deployment with PKI unconfigured answers 501 — a deployment-shape signal, not a client error.

vectors.title: Session introspection returns roles and bankId
vectors.description: GET /api/v1/auth/me is the canonical readiness probe for a session and the only way to discover the bankId the gateway will attribute the caller's writes to. A conformance runner reads roles here to decide which endpoint families the run may exercise.
vectors.notes: Only subject, issuer and roles are required. wallet, country, bankId and privacyGroup appear only when populated in the token. Two role namespaces coexist in the same roles array: ROLE_-prefixed names gate /api/v1 (ROLE_TREASURY, ROLE_COMMERCIAL_BANK, ROLE_GOVERNANCE...) and lowercase Keycloak realm roles gate /api/v2 (central_bank, commercial_bank, mlp). ROLE_CENTRAL_BANK_SCENARIO_B is a Go constant name and will never appear in a token.

vectors.title: Refresh with an empty body succeeds from the cookie
vectors.description: The platform document marks the request body required and refreshToken a required property. The delivered handler falls back to the refresh_token cookie when refreshToken is absent, so a browser-style client can refresh with an empty JSON body.
vectors.notes: Spec divergence mirrored in the contract description: a request-body validator built strictly from the schema would reject this call, which the gateway accepts. Both cookies are renewed.

vectors.title: Logout revokes the token and expires both cookies
vectors.description: Revokes the access token at Keycloak and expires the access_token and refresh_token cookies with Max-Age=-1. After this, auth-err-01 becomes the expected behaviour for the same jar.
vectors.notes: The contract declares a 400 on this operation because the platform does, but the route sits behind the cookie-auth middleware, so a request with no cookie is rejected with 401 before the handler runs (see auth-err-01).

vectors.title: No session cookie is 401 on every guarded route
vectors.description: The negative assertion that makes cookie authentication testable even against a stateless mock: a request to a CookieAuth-guarded route carrying no access_token cookie is rejected with 401 and a bare {error} body.

preconditions.session: empty cookie jar; no Authorization header

vectors.notes: Assert on the status code only. The /api/v1 error model is {error: "<free-form string>"} with no machine-readable code; the wording ('missing access_token cookie', 'invalid token', 'authentication required') varies by handler and is implementation detail.

vectors.title: Login without clientSecret is 400
vectors.description: Both clientId and clientSecret are required. Omitting either is a request-shape failure, not an authentication failure, and is answered 400 rather than 401.
vectors.notes: Distinguishing 400 from 401 here matters: a client that retries a 401 with fresh credentials will loop forever on a 400.

vectors.title: Wallet bind with a signature that does not verify is 401
vectors.description: A syntactically valid but cryptographically wrong nonce signature fails PKI verification. No cookies are set.

preconditions.signingKey: a key that does NOT match cert_pem

vectors.notes: The auth service is the one place on the surface that sometimes puts a code-like token in the free-form error field (NONCE_SIGNATURE_MISMATCH, INVALID_CERTIFICATE_CHAIN) and sometimes a human sentence — in the same field, on the same endpoint. Never match on it; assert 401.

vectors.title: Refresh with neither a body token nor a cookie is 400
vectors.description: The complement of auth-hp-05: with no refreshToken property AND no refresh_token cookie, the handler has no credential to exchange and answers 400, not 401.
vectors.notes: 401 is reserved for a refresh token that is present but invalid or expired.
